title: Where did it begin
hookLine: the yogis ask about the very beginning, and Nanak answers with wonder

lines: WHERE WAS THE VOID AT HOME?
cards: What was there before there was anything? Small children ask it at bedtime, usually right after the light goes off. Physicists ask it with chalk.
And in the Sidh Gosht, the yogis ask it of Nanak. So far they've asked about him: who he is, how he lives, why he travels, what he wears. Now they ask about everything.
What can you say about the beginning? Before anything was made, where was the void, the sunn, at home?

teach.b: The heart of Nanak's answer, in paraphrase: of the beginning, all one can speak of is wonder. The One dwelt then in itself, in the void, without end.

The word for wonder is bismaad, the word Sikhs use for awe so large it leaves you without anything to add. Notice what Nanak doesn't do. He doesn't hand the yogis a list of steps, first this, then that.

teach.h: NO STEPS, NO DATE, NO MECHANISM.
teach.b: He gives no date and no mechanism. Asked the biggest question there is, he gives a one-word answer: wonder. That's not a refusal.

It's a report. In this poem, the beginning is met with astonishment, not with a diagram. Then he takes the yogis' own word, sunn, the void, and doesn't argue with it; the word belonged to their own practice.
He agrees there was a void before all things. He just says who was there: the One, dwelling in itself.
The emptiness wasn't empty. Near the start of the Japji there's a similar move: the One before the ages, true in the beginning.
And elsewhere the Guru Granth Sahib speaks of a long darkness before creation, where only the divine order was. The texts don't try to make the beginning ordinary. They let it stay huge.
The coffee, the birdsong, the fact that there's anything at all instead of nothing: in this poem, the right first response to all of it is bismaad.

how: Sikhs speak of bismaad, wonder or awe, as a fitting response to the Creator and creation, and the Sidh Gosht's answer about the beginning is read in katha alongside the Japji's opening and the hymns of the time before creation.

games.q: what does “where did it begin” mean?
o: the yogis' list of steps by which the world was made
a hymn naming the day and year the world began
the yogis' question of the beginning, answered: only wonder

games.q: what's inside the answer — tap the pairs.

s: Nanak answers the question of the beginning with a step-by-step account
he says of the beginning, one can only speak of wonder.
Nanak accepts the yogis' word for the void, sunn
he agrees there was a void, and says the One dwelt in it, in itself.
in the answer, the void before creation was empty of everything
the One dwelt there; the emptiness wasn't empty.

games.q: the yogis ask you the biggest question there is: what can you say about the beginning? what does Nanak answer?
o: a list of what was made first.
that of the beginning, one can speak only of wonder.
that the question shouldn't be asked.
games.why: he answers with bismaad, wonder, and says the One dwelt in the void without end.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing within reach of your senses, your own hand, the light in the room, a sound outside, and look or listen as if it had only just appeared, letting the question come gently: why is this here at all, instead of nothing?
Don't try to answer, since Nanak didn't give the yogis a mechanism either; when the mind starts explaining, just come back to looking. If you pray, let that astonishment be the prayer, without words.

wordCard.voice: Where did it begin. The yogis' question about the beginning, and Nanak's answer: of that, one can only speak with wonder, and the One dwelt in the void. Today's word.

orig.note: bismaad: wonder, awe; Nanak's one-word answer about the beginning.

carryVoice: Your line: it began in wonder. Not with a diagram, but with astonishment. See you tomorrow.
